newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Pyongyang defector says he wants to avert war.
newsitem.headline: Pyongyang defector says he wants to avert war.

text.p: Flinging both arms high in a victory salute, North Korean defector Hwang Jang-yop arrived in South Korea on Sunday and declared his mission was to stop Pyongyang from launching a war.
Hwang, the most senior Pyongyang offical ever to betray his communist homeland, was presented with flowers after he arrived from the Philippines with an aide, Kim Duk-hong.

"I came to South Korea because I am convinced the only way out is to block war by joining hands with brothers in the South," he told reporters, his voice breaking with emotion, after landing at a military air base near Seoul.

Hwang and his aide raised their arms three times in triumph after emerging from a chartered Air Philippines Boeing 737. They smiled as they walked down red-carpetted stairs from the plane to the airport tarmac.

North Korea's top ideologue and the aide defected in Beijing on February 12 and had been in the Philippines since March 18. Their whereabouts in the Philippines had been a tight secret due to Manila's fears of Pyongyang hitmen.
"North Korea seems to think there is no option but to use the forces they have amassed," Hwang said in his statement read to reporters and broadcast on live television.
"The North Korean economy is almost paralysed. People are suffering from starvation and the government has no choice but to beg from international agencies," he said.
It was the first public glimpse of Hwang since he walked into a South Korean embassy compound in Beijing.
The defection embarrassed China by forcing it to choose between an old socialist ally and a new capitalist friend.
The Seoul foreign ministry thanked Beijing and Manila for their roles in Hwang's flight.
A ministry spokesman said South Korea "highly recognises the Chinese government, which treated his defection in accordance with international law and procedure".
"We also express deep appreciation to the Philippine government and the public for its friendship and cooperation," spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said.
A relieved Philippine President Fidel Ramos said he hoped the episode would boost chances of peace on the Korean Peninsula.
Philippine officials had imposed an information blackout on Hwang's journey to Seoul because of fears North Korea could try to intercept the flight.
"It's risky, very risky," Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said in a radio interview.

"Anything can happen during the three hour flight," another Philippine official said. "It would be easy to take off from Pyongyang. They are still in a Cold War. To the North Koreans, the life of that man no longer has any value.

Hwang was accompanied on the flight by a Philippine general, who formally handed the defectors over to Manila's ambassador in Seoul on arrival. The ambassador in turn passed the defector and his aide over to a South Korean security official.

The two defectors were welcomed at a brief ceremony by former South Korean prime minister Yoo Chang-soon, who attended the same high school as Hwang in Pyongyang before the Korean peninsula was divided after World War Two.

They were presented with bouquets of flowers by the wives of two prominent defectors, one a former Pyongyang diplomat in Zambia, who arrived last year, and the other a former foreign exchange dealer, who arrived in 1995.
The two Koreas have been locked in confrontation since the 1950-53 Korean War ended in a truce.
On Saturday, North Korea failed to resume talks for the second straight day with the United States and South Korea on a proposal for peace.
The future of the discussions in New York was uncertain.
